Centripetal and Centrifugal Force. A widespread misconception treats these as equal-and-opposite real forces, but only centripetal force is genuine. Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force or fictitious force that appears to act in a rotating reference frame but has no physical cause—it's an artifact of non-inertial observation, not a force that actually pulls outward.

Centripetal force is the real force directed toward the center of a circular path, required to keep an object in circular motion. Think of tension in a string, friction on a curve, or gravity keeping planets in orbit. Centrifugal force, by contrast, is not real but a perceived effect in rotating frames of reference. It describes the apparent outward acceleration experienced by an observer in that frame, due to the inertia of the object.

Newton's first law of motion explains the confusion perfectly. An object in circular motion tends to continue in a straight line, and the centripetal force continuously changes its direction. From a rotating observer's perspective, an outward force appears to act, but this is just inertia resisting the direction change. The centripetal acceleration depends on mass, velocity, and radius according to the formula a equals v squared divided by r. There is no corresponding centrifugal acceleration in inertial frames.

On a merry-go-round, for instance, the centripetal force from friction or tension pulls you toward the center. The sensation of being pushed outward is your inertia resisting the direction change, not a centrifugal force at all. Engineers and physicists do use the fictional centrifugal force as a practical tool in rotating reference frames, like in centrifuges, because it simplifies calculations in non-inertial frames. But it remains entirely fictitious, a mathematical convenience rather than a genuine physical phenomenon.
